In [[cryptography]], a '''Key Checksum Value''' (KCV) is the [[checksum]] of a [[Key_(cryptography)|cryptographic key]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://stackoverflow.com/questions/12228250/detecting-incorrect-key-using-aes-gcm-in-java|title=Cryptography - Detecting incorrect key using AES/GCM in JAVA}}</ref> It is used to validate the integrity of the key or compare keys without knowing their actual values. The KCV is computed by encrypting a block of bytes, each with value '00' or '01', with the cryptographic key and retaining the first 6 hexadecimal characters of the encrypted result. It is used in [[key management]] in different ciphering devices, such as [[SIM card|SIM-cards]] or [[Hardware security module|Hardware Security Modules (HSM)]].

In the [[GlobalPlatform]] technical specifications the KCV is defined for DES/3DES and AES keys as follows:<ref>GPC_SPE_034, [https://globalplatform.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/GPC_CardSpecification_v2.3.1_PublicRelease_CC.pdf "GlobalPlatform Card Specification 2.3.1"]
, ''[[Java_Card_OpenPlatform#GlobalPlatform|GlobalPlatform]]'', March 2018, Section B5</ref>

{{Blockquote
|text=For a DES key, the key check value is computed by encrypting 8 bytes, each with value '00', with the key to be checked and retaining the 3 highest-order bytes of the encrypted result. For a AES key, the key check value is computed by encrypting 16 bytes, each with value '01', with the key to be checked and retaining the 3 highest-order bytes of the encrypted result.
}}

The same definition is used by the [[GSMA]].<ref>[https://www.gsma.com/newsroom/wp-content/uploads/SGP.02_v3.1.pdf "Remote Provisioning Architecture for Embedded UICC 3.1"], ''[[GSMA]]'', May 2016, Annex F</ref>

== KCV for symmetric key management in retail financial services ==
The payments cards industry uses the following definition, as documented in requirement 15-1 of [[Payment card industry|PCI]] PIN Security standard.<ref>[https://docs-prv.pcisecuritystandards.org/PIN/Standard/PCI_PIN_Security_Requirements_Testing_v3_1.pdf PCI PIN Security, requirements and testing procedures version 3.1], [[Payment card industry|PCI]], March 2021, Requirement 15-1</ref> The same definitions can also be found in the [[ASC X9]] standards under [https://x9.org/standard-release-ansi-x9-24-1-2017/ ANSI x9.24-1-2017] Retail Financial Services Symmetric [[Key management|Key Management]] Part 1<ref>[https://x9.org/standard-release-ansi-x9-24-1-2017/ ANSI x9.24-1-2017 Retail Financial Services Symmetric Key Management Part 1], ASC X9, 2017, Annex A</ref><blockquote>Check values may be computed by two methods. [[TDEA]] may use either method. [[Advanced Encryption Standard|AES]] must only use the [[Cmac|CMAC]] method. In the first method, check values are computed by encrypting an all binary zeros block using the [[Key (cryptography)|key]] or component as the encryption key, using the leftmost n-bits of the result; where n is at most 24 bits (6 hexadecimal digits/3 bytes). In the second method the KCV is calculated by [[Message authentication code|MACing]] an all binary zeros block using the [[Cmac|CMAC]] algorithm as specified in [[ISO/IEC 9797-1|ISO 9797-1]] (see also [https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/38/b/upd1/final NIST SP 800-38B]). The check value will be the leftmost n-bits of the result, where n is at most 40 bits (10 hexadecimal digits). The [[block cipher]] used in the [[Cmac|CMAC]] function is the same as the [[block cipher]] of the key itself. A [[TDEA]] key or a component of a [[TDEA]] key will be [[Message authentication code|MACed]] using the [[TDEA]] block cipher, while a 128-bit [[Advanced Encryption Standard|AES]] key or component will be [[Message authentication code|MACed]] using the [[Advanced Encryption Standard|AES]]-128 [[block cipher]].</blockquote>
